newsitem.title: UK: England's top judge attacks govt sentencing plans.
newsitem.headline: England's top judge attacks govt sentencing plans.

text.p: England's top judge on Sunday attacked government plans for tougher sentencing for repeat offenders, saying courts should have more say in the matter.
The criticism is the latest in a string of attacks on Home Secretary Michael Howard, who is trying to bolster the ruling party's law-and-order credentials before the looming election.
But the Lord Chief Justice, Lord Bingham, also warned that he may personally challenge parts of Howard's crime bill when it comes before the House of Lords, parliament's upper chamber.
Bingham told television interviewer David Frost that judges had to be given more discretion than proposed by the government.

Howard's bill calls for minimum three-year terms for people convicted of repeated burglaries, a minimum seven-year sentence for persistent drug dealers and automatic life sentences for people convicted of repeated violent or sexual crimes.
Judges would only be able to sidestep minimum sentences in exceptional cases. But Bingham said this was too restrictive and judges should be able to consider whether a sentence was unjust.
"That would at least enable him to give effect to his sense of what the justice of the case demanded. That's what he's there for. He's a professional, paid to be expert in these matters...
"It's likely that there will be those who will seek to soften various of the hard lines of this bill in the House of Lords. It's possible I may be one of those," Bingham said.

The attack by Bingham, named in May after his predecessor retired because of ill health, follows bitter criticism of the bill by senior members of the ruling party including two former Conservative Home Secretaries, Douglas Hurd and Kenneth Baker.
Bingham's predecessor, Lord Taylor, also clashed with Howard over the sentencing plans, accusing the Home Secretary in his final House of Lords speech of "a denial of justice".
Prison reformers say the bill will dramatically increase the number of people in jail without doing anything to tackle crime.

Howard is also under fire from the opposition Labour Party, which accuses him of trying to push the bill through purely for electoral reasons. Labour is well ahead of the Conservatives in polls with just six months at most before the general election.
